title: The tragic consequence when we struggle to receive the Grace of God. Part 1
scripture_text: ‘’I do not set aside the grace of God, for if righteousness could be gained through the law, Christ died for nothing.
devotional:
‘’Meanwhile, the older son was in the field. When he came near the house, he heard music and dancing. So he called one of the servants and asked him what was going on. ‘Your brother has come,’ he replied, ‘and your father has killed the fattened calf because he has him back safe and sound.’ The older brother became angry and refused to go in. So his father went out and pleaded with him. But he answered his father, ‘Look! All these years I’ve been slaving for you and never disobeyed your orders. Yet you never gave me even a young goat so I could celebrate with my friends. But when this son of yours who has squandered your property with prostitutes comes home, you kill the fattened calf for him!’ My son,’ the father said, ‘you are always with me, and everything I have is yours. But we had to celebrate and be glad, because this brother of yours was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found.”

The etiquette of unwanted Christmas gifts

I wonder did you get any presents at Christmas you didn’t really want? If so, what did you do with them and how do you avoid hurting the feelings of those who took the time and trouble to buy, wrap and give you a gift they thought you would like – or even love!

Jesus is God’s gift to us not just at Christmas but throughout all time, but what happens when the unwanted gift is the grace of God?

This may be a difficult concept to get our heads around, but there are some people who find it difficult if not impossible to receive grace. Paul spoke of those who ‘set aside’ the grace of God. Galatians 2:21. Even more surprisingly there are many people who want to follow Jesus find it hard to receive grace. No one would ever say, ‘I don’t want the grace of God,’ it is not something we would ever verbalise, but we can develop an attitude that says, I can solve this problem, or, this work/ministry depends on me, and we see ourselves as indispensable. The older brother in our text, did not understand grace, or his need of it. There will never be a circumstance or a day in our lives where we will not need the grace of God.

We want to look at two questions, 1. Why would people refuse grace? 2. What are the consequences of refusing grace?

Writing to the Christians in Galatia, Paul said, ‘I do not set aside the grace of God, for if righteousness could be gained through the law, Christ died for nothing.’ Galatians 2:21.

The word translated ‘set aside,’ is atheteō which means to reject, it was used to describe the annulling of a will, or to treat something as having no value. In the Greek translation of the Old Testament, the word is often translated unfaithful or betray, to rebel and scorn. The Christians in Galatia had developed a resistant attitude towards God’s grace; they were beginning to treat the grace of God as an unwanted gift.

Let’s try and examine the attitudes and mindset that prevents a person from receiving the grace of God. We want to look at the story of the elder brother in the parable of the Prodigal Son.

This is one of the best known parables of Jesus, but although it is well known, I don’t think it is very well understood. When you read the parables of Jesus you should always look for the ‘sting in the tale,’ the ending is never quite what you expect or hope for. So when you read the story of the prodigal son you are surprised to realise that the real prodigal is not the younger son who squandered his inheritance, but the elder brother who squandered his life, because he refused to understand grace, or receive it.

Before we look at this story, I think it is important to mention the cultural context of the story. One commentator Kenneth Bailey points out, that it is hard for us to imagine how insulting the older son's behaviour was to his father. He suggests that we imagine a wealthy man having a black tie, candle lit dinner for prestigious guests, only to have his eldest son show up at the door unshaven, without shirt and shoes, and begin to verbally attack the father. According to Bailey, this analogy is too mild to convey the revolting nature of the older son's behaviour. He suggests that the behaviour of this son is actually more cutting than the behaviour of the youngest son at the beginning of the story. At least that disrespect was done in private.

We are going look at his attitudes that made it impossible for him to receive the grace of his father, and how the lack of grace affected him.

The elder son ran from the father into the activity of service.

The first thing we are told about the elder son is, ‘Meanwhile, the elder son was in field.’ This is not a throw away statement but a succinct description of how the elder son lived, and what he lived for. The field was a symbol that summed up his life. He was the kind of person who tried to medicate his pain by doing, and found his value and significance in what he achieved. He buried himself in doing to compensate for his poor relationship with his father. In Christian circles people often fall into the trap of becoming too busy that they cannot really grasp what is important to the father.

Hard work is a good thing, but when our work becomes a place where we hide from dealing with the reality of our own hearts, then it is wrong, and this was the sin of the elder brother. Sometimes we use Christian service as a smoke screen to hide the real us.

When we fall into the mindset that puts too high a value on service we become incapable of receiving or enjoying the grace of God because our lives will be all about us trying to meet our own needs and medicating our own pain. Serving God is a wonderful thing if it is not being used to replace intimacy with the father. We will only experience healing and fullness in the embrace of the father. Sometimes our emptiness or baroness can drive us into service. If we were in the world we might turn to drugs, alcohol, materialism or some other vice to medicate our pain. Often Christian service can become ‘vice like,’ for it is used as means of anaesthetising ourselves from the pain of reality.
prayer: Father may I never use Christian service to anaesthetise my pain but let me be healed by your grace.
